easy.text: Which ancient civilization, known for detailed pottery and monumental adobe pyramids, flourished on the northern coast of Peru long before the Inca Empire?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Moche thrived on Peru's north coast roughly from 100 to 700 CE, centuries before the Inca rose to power.
The Inca came many centuries later and built their empire in the Andes highlands, not the earlier north-coast Moche culture.
The Aztecs were centered in Mesoamerica (modern Mexico), an entirely different region from coastal Peru.
The Maya were centered in Mesoamerica, not the Peruvian coast where the Moche lived.

medium.text: A famous 1987 archaeological discovery in northern Peru, filled with gold and silver regalia and left largely untouched by looters, revealed the tomb of which Moche figure?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Lord of Sipan's tomb offered an extraordinary look at Moche wealth, craftsmanship, and religious hierarchy.
Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered in Egypt in 1922, an entirely different civilization and century.
That refers to Qin Shi Huang's tomb complex in China, unrelated to the Moche of Peru.
Pachacuti was a later Inca emperor, not a Moche ruler.

hard.text: Which two massive adobe (mud-brick) structures, dedicated to the sun and the moon, formed the ceremonial heart of the Moche civilization's capital?

options.text: Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna
options.feedback: Correct -- these two great adobe pyramids anchored Moche religious and political life on Peru's north coast.

options.text: The Pyramid of the Sun and Pyramid of the Moon at Teotihuacan
options.feedback: Those similarly named pyramids belong to Teotihuacan in Mexico, a completely different civilization.
Those are later Inca stone structures near Cuzco, not the Moche's mud-brick monuments.
Those are Maya sites in Mesoamerica, unrelated to the Moche of coastal Peru.

easy.easy: This culture's stirrup-spout pottery and coastal adobe pyramids date centuries before the Inca rose to power in the Andes.
easy.medium: This culture predates the Inca by many centuries and is known for elaborate ceramic art.
easy.hard: This civilization lived along the northern coast of the South American country later ruled by the Inca.

medium.easy: This 1987 discovery in northern Peru revealed a richly adorned ruler's burial, distinct from Egyptian or Chinese royal tomb finds.
medium.medium: This tomb, found in Peru in the 1980s, belonged to a pre-Inca warrior-priest ruler.
medium.hard: This discovery was an unlooted royal tomb filled with gold and silver ornaments.

hard.easy: These two adobe monuments, one for the sun and one for the moon, are unrelated to the similarly named pyramids at Teotihuacan or to later Inca stonework.
hard.medium: These mud-brick pyramids formed the Moche capital's religious center, distinct from Mexico's stone pyramids of the same names.
hard.hard: These two structures were dedicated to the sun and the moon.

topic: the Chavin culture of the Andes

easy.text: Chavin de Huantar, an ancient ceremonial center famous for its elaborate stone carvings, is located in which South American mountain range?

options.feedback: Correct -- Chavin de Huantar sits high in the Peruvian Andes and gave its name to the broader Chavin culture.
The Alps are in Europe, an entirely different continent from the Andean site of Chavin de Huantar.
The Himalayas are in Asia, unrelated to the Andean Chavin culture of South America.
The Rocky Mountains are in North America, not the South American range home to Chavin culture.

medium.text: Chavin artwork is especially known for stylized carvings of which powerful animal, believed to hold deep religious significance?

options.feedback: Correct -- feline imagery, especially jaguar-like faces and fangs, pervades Chavin stone carvings and iconography.
Raptor imagery does appear in Chavin art, but its most emphasized and recognizable motif is the feline, not the eagle alone.
Horses were not present in the Americas until Europeans introduced them much later -- they play no role in Chavin imagery.
Elephants never existed in South America, so they have no place in Chavin religious art.

hard.text: Because Chavin's distinctive religious iconography and artistic style spread widely across the Andes without evidence of military conquest, archaeologists often describe it as what kind of culture?

options.text: A 'horizon' culture, spread mainly through shared religion, art, and trade rather than conquest
options.feedback: Correct -- the 'Chavin Horizon' describes how its influence spread through belief and exchange rather than warfare.

options.text: A military empire that conquered its neighbors, similar to the later Inca
options.feedback: Unlike the Inca, Chavin's influence is not attributed to military conquest -- it spread through shared religious and artistic ideas.

options.text: A maritime empire built on overseas colonization
options.feedback: Chavin's influence spread across the Andean highlands and coast through trade and belief, not overseas colonization.

options.text: A nomadic confederation without any fixed ceremonial centers
options.feedback: Chavin was centered on a major fixed temple complex at Chavin de Huantar, not a nomadic society.

easy.easy: This mountain range runs along the western edge of South America.
easy.medium: This range is home to later civilizations like the Inca, as well as much earlier ones.
easy.hard: This range stretches the length of western South America and cradled cultures from ancient Chavin through the much later Inca.

medium.easy: This animal is a large, powerful cat known for its strength and stealth.
medium.medium: This big cat's fanged, snarling face appears repeatedly in Chavin stone carvings.
medium.hard: This predator's stylized face and fangs recur throughout Chavin religious art, distinct from bird or livestock imagery from Old World cultures.

hard.easy: Think about how ideas can spread through shared belief and trade instead of armies.
hard.medium: This term describes influence spreading through religion and trade, not soldiers and conquest.
hard.hard: This term distinguishes cultural and religious diffusion across a wide region from empire-building through military campaigns, overseas colonies, or nomadic wandering.

topic: Angkor Wat and the Khmer Empire

easy.text: Angkor Wat, one of the largest religious monuments in the world, is located in which present-day country?

options.feedback: Correct -- Angkor Wat sits near Siem Reap in modern Cambodia, once the heart of the Khmer Empire.
Thailand borders the region but Angkor Wat itself lies within modern Cambodia.
Vietnam lies to the east of Cambodia and was not home to the Khmer capital of Angkor.
Indonesia is a separate archipelago nation, not the location of Angkor Wat.

medium.text: Angkor Wat was originally built as a temple dedicated to which Hindu god, before gradually becoming a Buddhist site over the centuries?

options.feedback: Correct -- Angkor Wat was originally consecrated as a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu.
Many earlier Khmer temples honored Shiva, but Angkor Wat itself was dedicated to Vishnu.
Brahma was not the deity Angkor Wat was consecrated to -- that was Vishnu.
Ganesha is a widely worshipped Hindu god, but Angkor Wat's dedication was specifically to Vishnu.

hard.text: Which Khmer king commissioned the construction of Angkor Wat in the early 12th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- Suryavarman II commissioned Angkor Wat as his state temple and likely mausoleum in the early 1100s.
Jayavarman VII built Angkor Thom and the Bayon temple decades later -- Angkor Wat itself was Suryavarman II's project.
Jayavarman II is credited with founding the Khmer Empire centuries earlier, not with building Angkor Wat.
Indravarman I ruled much earlier and built other Khmer monuments, not Angkor Wat.

easy.easy: This Southeast Asian country is home to the ancient Angkor temple complex.
easy.medium: This country lies between Thailand and Vietnam in mainland Southeast Asia.
easy.hard: This country's name is closely tied to the Khmer people who built the great temple complex near modern Siem Reap.

medium.easy: This god is one of the principal deities of Hinduism, often depicted with four arms.
medium.medium: This deity is part of the Hindu trinity alongside Brahma and Shiva.
medium.hard: This deity, not Shiva or Brahma, was the one Angkor Wat's builders chose to honor in its original dedication.

hard.easy: This king's name begins with a word meaning 'sun' in Sanskrit -- a prefix none of the other three rulers listed share.
hard.medium: This king ruled in the early 1100s, before the later ruler who built Angkor Thom.
hard.hard: This king, distinct from the founder of the Khmer Empire and from the later builder of Angkor Thom and the Bayon, is credited specifically with Angkor Wat itself.

easy.text: The Srivijaya Empire was a powerful maritime trading empire based on which Indonesian island?

options.feedback: Correct -- Srivijaya was centered near modern Palembang on the island of Sumatra.
Java was later home to the Majapahit Empire, not the earlier Srivijaya, which was based on Sumatra.
Borneo was not the seat of Srivijaya's power -- that was the island of Sumatra.
Bali is a much smaller island and was not the center of the Srivijaya Empire.

medium.text: Srivijaya's control over which strategic waterway made it central to trade between India and China?

options.feedback: Correct -- controlling this narrow, busy passage let Srivijaya tax and profit from ships moving between India and China.
The Strait of Hormuz is near the Persian Gulf, far from Srivijaya's Southeast Asian territory.
The Bosphorus links the Black Sea and Mediterranean near Constantinople, unrelated to Southeast Asian trade routes.
The Sunda Strait lies further south between Sumatra and Java, but it was the Strait of Malacca that defined Srivijaya's dominance.

hard.text: A famous Chinese Buddhist monk traveled to Srivijaya in the 7th century to study Buddhist scriptures there and later wrote an account of the empire. Who was this monk?

options.feedback: Correct -- Yijing studied at Srivijaya's Buddhist centers of learning and documented the empire in his writings.
Xuanzang famously traveled overland to India to study Buddhism, not to Srivijaya by sea.
Faxian traveled to India generations earlier and is not the monk associated with studying in Srivijaya.
Zheng He was a Ming Dynasty admiral centuries later, not a Buddhist scholar-monk studying in Srivijaya.

easy.easy: This island is home to the modern Indonesian city of Palembang.
easy.medium: This large island lies west of Java in the Indonesian archipelago.
easy.hard: This island's coastal city of Palembang was the seat of a maritime trading power that controlled nearby shipping lanes.

medium.easy: This narrow passage lies between the Malay Peninsula and the island of Sumatra.
medium.medium: This waterway was the key shipping lane linking Indian Ocean and South China Sea trade.
medium.hard: This narrow, heavily trafficked passage between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra -- not a strait near the Middle East or Europe -- was Srivijaya's economic lifeline.

hard.easy: This monk traveled by sea and spent years studying Buddhism in Southeast Asia.
hard.medium: This monk's journey and studies took him through Srivijaya on his way to and from India.
hard.hard: This monk, distinct from the famous overland traveler to India and from a much later Ming naval admiral, documented his years of study at Srivijaya's Buddhist institutions.

easy.text: The Majapahit Empire, one of the last major Hindu-Buddhist empires of Southeast Asia, was centered on which island?

options.feedback: Correct -- Majapahit's capital and heartland were on the island of Java.
Sumatra was home to the earlier Srivijaya Empire, not Majapahit's core territory.
Borneo was not the center of Majapahit power -- that was the island of Java.
Sulawesi lies further east and was not Majapahit's core territory.

medium.text: Majapahit reached its greatest extent and influence during the reign of which king, working alongside his powerful chief minister Gajah Mada?

options.feedback: Correct -- under Hayam Wuruk and Gajah Mada, Majapahit's influence stretched across much of maritime Southeast Asia.
Raden Wijaya founded Majapahit generations earlier -- its peak came later, under Hayam Wuruk.
Kertanegara ruled the earlier Singhasari kingdom, which predated Majapahit.
Suryavarman II was a Khmer king who built Angkor Wat, unrelated to Majapahit in Java.

hard.text: Because Majapahit's sphere of influence once stretched across much of the modern Indonesian archipelago and beyond, the empire is often invoked in modern Indonesia as what?

options.text: A historical symbol of territorial unity for the modern Indonesian nation
options.feedback: Correct -- Majapahit's wide reach is frequently cited as a precedent for Indonesia's modern national boundaries and identity.

options.text: Evidence of early Islamic governance in the region
options.feedback: Majapahit was a Hindu-Buddhist empire -- widespread Islamic governance in the archipelago came later, after Majapahit's decline.

options.text: The origin of Indonesia's modern parliamentary system
options.feedback: Indonesia's parliamentary system is a 20th-century development, unrelated to Majapahit's governance structure.

options.text: The source of the Indonesian language's grammar
options.feedback: Modern Indonesian is based on Malay, not directly derived from Majapahit-era Javanese governance.

easy.easy: This island is also home to Indonesia's modern capital region and largest population.
easy.medium: This island lies east of Sumatra and was the heartland of a later, different empire than Srivijaya.
easy.hard: This island, distinct from Sumatra's earlier maritime power, was the heartland of a later empire that reached its peak in the 14th century.

medium.easy: This ruler worked alongside a famous chief minister who swore to unify the archipelago.
medium.medium: This king reigned during Majapahit's golden age, well after its founding.
medium.hard: This king, not the empire's founder nor an earlier rival kingdom's ruler, presided over Majapahit's widest territorial reach alongside his chief minister.

hard.easy: Think about how a powerful, far-reaching ancient kingdom might be remembered by a much later nation.
hard.medium: This role is about national symbolism and unity, not religion, government structure, or language.
hard.hard: This role concerns how a sprawling pre-colonial empire's reach is used today as a symbolic precedent, distinct from religious, linguistic, or governmental claims.

easy.text: Which of the following are true about the Byzantine Empire? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It was the continuation of the Roman Empire's eastern half
options.feedback: Correct -- after Rome's western half fell, its eastern half continued on as the Byzantine Empire.
Correct -- Constantinople served as the Byzantine Empire's capital for over a thousand years.
Charlemagne founded the later Carolingian Empire in Western Europe -- he did not found the Byzantine Empire.

options.text: It fell in 476 CE, the same year as the Western Roman Empire
options.feedback: 476 CE only marks the Western Roman Empire's fall -- the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire survived for nearly another thousand years, until 1453.

medium.text: Which of the following accurately describe the Byzantine Empire's institutions and culture? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It preserved and continued Roman legal and administrative traditions
options.feedback: Correct -- Byzantine emperors maintained and adapted Roman law and bureaucracy for centuries.

options.text: Its dominant religion, after its early centuries, was Eastern Orthodox Christianity
options.feedback: Correct -- the Byzantine Empire became a center of Eastern Orthodox Christian practice and theology.

options.text: It abandoned Roman legal traditions in favor of an entirely unrelated legal system
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire didn't discard Roman law -- it preserved and adapted Roman legal and administrative traditions for centuries.

options.text: It was governed by an elected parliament with no monarch
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire was ruled by emperors, not by an elected parliamentary system.

hard.text: Which of the following accurately distinguish the Byzantine Empire from the Western Roman Empire that collapsed in 476 CE? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It survived for roughly another thousand years after Rome's western half fell
options.feedback: Correct -- the Byzantine Empire endured until 1453, nearly a millennium after the west's collapse.

options.text: Its dominant language gradually shifted from Latin to Greek
options.feedback: Correct -- over time, Greek became the empire's primary administrative and cultural language.

options.text: It was conquered by the Visigoths in the 5th century
options.feedback: The Visigoths were involved in the Western Roman Empire's fall, not the Byzantine (eastern) empire's downfall.

options.text: It never faced any external military threats until 1453
options.feedback: The Byzantine Empire faced centuries of invasions and wars long before its final fall in 1453.

easy.easy: One correct answer is about which older empire this one continued from; the other is about its famous capital city.
easy.medium: Both true statements involve Rome's legacy and a city straddling Europe and Asia.
easy.hard: Think broadly about this empire's deep historical roots and the general part of the world where its power was centered, rather than any single ruler's name or an unrelated continent.

medium.easy: One correct answer is about law and government; the other is about religion.
medium.medium: Both true statements involve carrying forward Roman traditions and adopting a particular branch of Christianity.
medium.hard: Think broadly about which institutions carried over from the past and which faith became dominant, rather than any claim about discarding the old system entirely or ruling without a monarch.

hard.easy: One correct answer is about how long it lasted; the other is about its main language changing over time.
hard.medium: Both true statements involve the empire's long survival and a linguistic shift, not who conquered the west or how peaceful its history was.
hard.hard: Think broadly about how this empire's lifespan and everyday culture set it apart from its western counterpart, rather than any single invading group or how often conflict arose.

easy.text: Byzantine Emperor Justinian I is best known for commissioning a comprehensive compilation of Roman law known as what?

options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian ordered scholars to compile and organize centuries of Roman law into this influential code.
The Twelve Tables were an much earlier Roman law code, from the early Roman Republic, not Justinian's compilation.
The Edict of Milan was Emperor Constantine's earlier decree on religious tolerance, not a legal code.
The Nicene Creed is a statement of Christian religious belief, not a body of civil law.

medium.text: Justinian's military campaigns, led by his general Belisarius, were primarily aimed at achieving what overarching goal?

options.text: Reconquering the lost western territories of the former Roman Empire
options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian sought to restore Roman rule over regions like Italy and North Africa that had fallen to other powers.

options.text: Converting the empire's population to Islam
options.feedback: Islam did not yet exist during Justinian's reign in the 6th century -- his goal was western reconquest.

options.text: Establishing new trade colonies in China
options.feedback: Justinian's campaigns focused on Mediterranean territories, not establishing colonies in East Asia.

options.text: Conquering the entirety of the Persian Empire
options.feedback: Justinian fought costly wars with Persia but his primary strategic goal was reclaiming the lost Roman west.

hard.text: Justinian's legal code was organized into several parts; which part was specifically intended as an introductory textbook for law students?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Institutes summarized legal principles in a form designed for teaching students.
The Digest was a large compilation of earlier jurists' legal opinions, not the student textbook portion.
The Codex compiled imperial laws and decrees, not the introductory teaching text.
The Novellae collected new laws issued after the main code was completed, not the student textbook.

easy.easy: This achievement is a massive legal compilation, not a building or a military campaign.
easy.medium: This is a body of law, distinct from earlier Roman codes or unrelated religious and imperial edicts.
easy.hard: This achievement organized and preserved a vast body of existing law under one ruler's direction -- think about the general type of large-scale intellectual project this represents, rather than any specific era or document name.

medium.easy: Think about restoring old territory rather than gaining brand-new lands far away.
medium.medium: This goal involved reclaiming lands the empire had already once ruled, in the west.
medium.hard: Think about the general type of ambition this represents -- looking backward to restore something once held, rather than looking outward to gain something entirely new.

hard.easy: This part was meant for students just learning the law, not practicing judges.
hard.medium: This part was a simplified summary for teaching, distinct from the larger scholarly compilations.
hard.hard: Think about which audience this particular part of the code was written for, and what kind of document serves that audience, rather than the specific alternative parts by name.

easy.text: The Hagia Sophia, famous for its massive dome, was originally built as what type of structure?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Hagia Sophia was built as a grand Byzantine Christian cathedral in Constantinople.
It was later converted into a mosque after the Ottoman conquest, but it was originally built as a Christian cathedral.
It was never built as a bathhouse -- its original purpose was as a grand Christian cathedral.
It served a religious, not residential, purpose from the start, as a Christian cathedral.

medium.text: The Hagia Sophia was commissioned by which Byzantine emperor and completed in the 6th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- Justinian I had the Hagia Sophia built, completing it in 537 CE.
Constantine founded Constantinople two centuries earlier, but Justinian I commissioned the Hagia Sophia itself.
Theodosius II built an earlier cathedral on the site, but the grand structure standing today was Justinian's project.
Basil II ruled centuries after the Hagia Sophia's construction, not the emperor who commissioned it.

hard.text: After the Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453, the Hagia Sophia was converted into what, before later becoming a museum in the 20th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Ottomans converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque, adding minarets and Islamic religious features.
It retained a religious function under Ottoman rule as a mosque, rather than becoming a military fortress.
The building continued to serve a religious purpose as a mosque, not a commercial marketplace.
It functioned as a place of worship, a mosque, rather than a library, following the Ottoman conquest.

easy.easy: This structure's original purpose was religious worship for Christians.
easy.medium: This building served as the seat of the Byzantine church's central cathedral.
easy.hard: This building's original religious use came before it was later converted to serve a different faith following a conquest; it was not a secular structure like a bathhouse or a palace.

medium.easy: This emperor also commissioned a famous compilation of Roman law.
medium.medium: This emperor reigned in the 6th century and rebuilt this structure after riots damaged an earlier version.
medium.hard: This emperor, distinct from the founder of Constantinople two centuries earlier and from a much later ruler, is the one credited with completing the standing structure in 537 CE.

hard.easy: This new use was religious, tied to the faith of the conquering empire.
hard.medium: Minarets were added to the building for this new religious purpose.
hard.hard: This new function, under Ottoman rule, was religious in nature -- distinct from a defensive fortress, a commercial marketplace, or a repository of books.

topic: the Rashidun Caliphate and early Islamic expansion

easy.text: Which of the following were among the first four caliphs of the Rashidun Caliphate, who led the Muslim community after the Prophet Muhammad's death? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Abu Bakr became the first Rashidun caliph after Muhammad's death in 632 CE.
Correct -- Umar was the second Rashidun caliph, overseeing major early conquests.
Suleiman was an Ottoman sultan who ruled nearly a thousand years later, not one of the Rashidun caliphs.
Saladin was a much later Ayyubid sultan famous for opposing the Crusaders, not a Rashidun caliph.

medium.text: Which of the following are true about the Rashidun Caliphate's early military conquests? (Select all that apply)

options.text: It rapidly expanded beyond the Arabian Peninsula into former Byzantine and Persian territory
options.feedback: Correct -- within decades, Rashidun armies conquered vast lands once held by Byzantium and Persia.

options.text: It brought about the total collapse of the Sassanid Persian Empire
options.feedback: Correct -- the Sassanid Empire was completely overrun and ended by Rashidun conquests.

options.text: It never expanded beyond the Arabian Peninsula
options.feedback: The Rashidun Caliphate expanded dramatically beyond Arabia, into the Levant, Egypt, and Persia.

options.text: It was primarily a naval empire with little land expansion
options.feedback: The Rashidun conquests were driven primarily by land armies, not naval power.

hard.text: Which of the following accurately describe the Rashidun Caliphate specifically, as distinct from the later Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Its caliphs succeeded one another through selection among early companions of Muhammad, rather than hereditary dynastic succession
options.feedback: Correct -- unlike the later hereditary caliphates, the Rashidun caliphs were chosen from among Muhammad's early companions.

options.text: It ended with the assassination of Ali and the rise of the Umayyad dynasty
options.feedback: Correct -- Ali's assassination in 661 CE marked the Rashidun era's end and the start of Umayyad rule.

options.text: It moved its capital permanently to Baghdad
options.feedback: Baghdad was founded and became a capital under the later Abbasid Caliphate, not the Rashidun era.

options.text: It was ruled by a hereditary dynasty founded by Muawiyah
options.feedback: Muawiyah founded the hereditary Umayyad dynasty after the Rashidun period ended, not during it.

easy.easy: One correct answer is the very first leader after Muhammad; the other led major conquests as the second leader.
easy.medium: Both correct answers ruled in the 7th century, right after Muhammad's death, not centuries later.
easy.hard: Both correct answers belong to the earliest generation of Muslim leaders, distinct from a much later Ottoman sultan and a later Ayyubid sultan famous for the Crusades era.

medium.easy: Both correct statements describe expansion into former Byzantine and Persian lands and the complete downfall of a specific Persian dynasty, not a claim of staying confined to Arabia or of relying mainly on naval power.
medium.medium: Both true statements involve conquest beyond Arabia and the end of a major Persian dynasty.
medium.hard: One correct answer is about how far the conquests reached; the other is about a Persian empire's fate.

hard.easy: Both correct statements concern a selection-based (not hereditary) leadership method and the violent end of this era, distinct from a later capital city and a later hereditary dynasty's founding.
hard.medium: Both true statements involve a non-hereditary succession method and a violent transition to the next caliphate.
hard.hard: One correct answer is about how leaders were chosen; the other is about how this era ended.

easy.text: The Umayyad Caliphate, one of the largest empires in history, established its capital in which city?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Umayyads made Damascus their capital, ruling a vast empire from this Syrian city.
Baghdad became the capital under the later Abbasid Caliphate, not the Umayyads.
Cairo rose to prominence under later Islamic dynasties, not as the Umayyad capital.
Mecca remained Islam's holiest city, but the Umayyad seat of political power was Damascus.

medium.text: The Umayyad Caliphate's territory stretched from the Iberian Peninsula in the west to which region in the east?

options.feedback: Correct -- Umayyad territory reached as far east as the Indus valley in present-day Pakistan.
Umayyad rule never extended to China's coast -- its eastern edge reached the Indus valley.
Japan was far beyond Umayyad reach -- its eastern border was the Indus valley.
Australia was entirely unconnected to the Umayyad world -- its territory extended only as far as the Indus valley in the east.

hard.text: After being overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution in 750 CE, a surviving Umayyad prince fled westward and founded a new Umayyad state in which region?

options.feedback: Correct -- Abd al-Rahman I escaped to Iberia and established the Emirate of Cordoba, continuing Umayyad rule there.
Persia became the heartland of the new Abbasid Caliphate, not a refuge for the fleeing Umayyad prince.
The surviving Umayyad prince passed through parts of North Africa but ultimately established his new state in Iberia, not Egypt.
Anatolia was largely Byzantine territory at the time, not where the exiled Umayyad prince founded his new state.

easy.easy: This city is in modern Syria and gives its name to a well-known style of early Islamic mosque architecture.
easy.medium: This city was the political heart of the Umayyad dynasty, distinct from the later Abbasid capital.
easy.hard: This Syrian city, not the later Abbasid capital or Islam's holiest city, was where the Umayyads ruled their vast empire.

medium.easy: This river flows through present-day Pakistan.
medium.medium: This region marks the far eastern edge of Umayyad expansion, in South Asia.
medium.hard: This river valley, not a coastal region of China, Japan, or Australia, marked the eastern limit of Umayyad territorial reach.

hard.easy: This region is in southwestern Europe, once home to a long-lasting Islamic state.
hard.medium: This region became home to a new Umayyad emirate centered at Cordoba.
hard.hard: This region, distinct from the new Abbasid heartland in Persia, from Egypt, and from Byzantine Anatolia, became the refuge where Umayyad rule continued for centuries more.

topic: the Abbasid Caliphate and the House of Wisdom

easy.text: The Abbasid Caliphate, which overthrew the Umayyads in 750 CE, established its new capital in which city?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Abbasids built Baghdad as their new capital, which became a major center of learning and trade.
Damascus had been the Umayyad capital -- the Abbasids moved the seat of power to Baghdad instead.
Cairo rose to prominence under other later dynasties, not as the Abbasid capital.
Medina was significant in early Islamic history, but the Abbasid capital was Baghdad.

medium.text: The House of Wisdom, a major intellectual center in Baghdad, was especially known for what activity that preserved and expanded classical knowledge?

options.text: Translating Greek, Persian, and Indian scholarly texts into Arabic
options.feedback: Correct -- scholars at the House of Wisdom translated and built upon works from many earlier civilizations.

options.text: Printing the first books using movable type
options.feedback: Movable-type printing in this form developed elsewhere and much later -- the House of Wisdom's core activity was translation and scholarship.

options.text: Minting the very first coins in history
options.feedback: Coinage predates the House of Wisdom by many centuries -- its defining activity was translation and scholarly research.

options.text: Building the first observatories anywhere in the world
options.feedback: Observatories existed in earlier civilizations too -- the House of Wisdom's central legacy was its translation movement.

hard.text: The House of Wisdom is credited with reaching its greatest prominence as a formal institution under the patronage of which Abbasid caliph in the early 9th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- al-Ma'mun is widely credited with formally establishing and expanding the House of Wisdom as a major center of scholarship.
Al-Mansur founded Baghdad itself decades earlier, but the House of Wisdom's peak is credited to al-Ma'mun.
Al-Mutawakkil ruled later in the 9th century, after the House of Wisdom's height under al-Ma'mun.
Al-Wathiq ruled after al-Ma'mun's era -- it was al-Ma'mun who is credited with the institution's formal rise.

easy.easy: This city sits along the Tigris River in modern Iraq.
easy.medium: This city became a major Abbasid center of trade and scholarship, distinct from the earlier Umayyad capital.
easy.hard: This city rose along a major Mesopotamian river under the dynasty that seized power in a mid-8th-century revolution, later becoming renowned for its intellectual life.

medium.easy: This activity involved converting texts from one language into Arabic.
medium.medium: Scholars here worked to bring older works, written in other languages, into wider Arabic circulation.
medium.hard: This activity bridged the learning of earlier, distant civilizations into the Arabic-speaking world, rather than any single invention sometimes wrongly credited to this era.

hard.easy: This caliph reigned in the early 800s, after the city of Baghdad was already founded.
hard.medium: This caliph is often specifically credited with formalizing this scholarly institution, distinct from the city's founder.
hard.hard: This caliph, ruling in the early 9th century and distinct from Baghdad's original founder and from later caliphs, is most closely tied to the House of Wisdom's peak.

topic: the Golden Age of Islamic science and scholarship

easy.text: Which of these fields saw major advances during the Islamic Golden Age (roughly the 8th through 13th centuries)? (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- scholars like Al-Khwarizmi made foundational contributions to algebra during this era.
Correct -- physicians like Ibn Sina produced medical texts used for centuries across the Islamic world and Europe.

options.text: The invention of the steam engine

easy.text: The Reconquista refers to the centuries-long effort by Christian kingdoms to retake control of which peninsula from Muslim rule?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Reconquista describes the long campaign across the Iberian Peninsula, home to modern Spain and Portugal.
The Italian Peninsula was not the site of the Reconquista -- that took place on the Iberian Peninsula.
The Balkans were a different region entirely, later contested between Christian kingdoms and the Ottoman Empire, not the Reconquista's setting.
The Arabian Peninsula was the birthplace of Islam, not the site of the Reconquista campaigns.

medium.text: The Reconquista formally concluded in 1492 with the fall of which city, the last Muslim stronghold in Iberia?

options.feedback: Correct -- the fall of Granada in 1492 marked the end of nearly 800 years of Muslim rule in Iberia.
Cordoba had fallen to Christian forces centuries earlier -- Granada was the last stronghold, falling in 1492.
Toledo fell to Christian forces long before 1492 -- Granada was the final Muslim stronghold.
Seville fell in the 13th century, well before Granada, which held out as the last Muslim stronghold until 1492.

hard.text: Which joint Christian monarchs completed the Reconquista by conquering Granada in 1492?

options.text: Charles V and his mother Joanna

Philip II ruled decades after 1492 -- Ferdinand and Isabella were the monarchs who conquered Granada.
Alfonso X ruled Castile centuries earlier and did not complete the Reconquista -- that was Ferdinand and Isabella.

easy.text: The Great Schism of 1054 formally divided Christianity into which two major branches?
